candidates.title: Baseline and longitudinal changes in blood biomarkers for predicting clinical outcomes in pirfenidone-treated idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: a prospective observational study.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study investigated blood biomarkers for predicting lung function decline or disease progression in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) receiving pirfenidone.
METHODS: Data from a multicenter prospective observational study in South Korea were analyzed. Patients with available blood samples at baseline and 6 months were followed up for 12 months. We assessed the predictive value of baseline levels and 6-month changes in nine biomarkers for forced vital capacity (FVC) deterioration and disease progression. FVC deterioration was defined as an absolute decline of ≥ 10% points in FVC % predicted at 12 months, while disease progression included FVC deterioration, hospitalization, or death.
RESULTS: A total of 118 patients were included, with a mean age of 68.9 years and 82.2% being men. Median follow-up and treatment duration were 350 days. Greater FVC decline was observed in patients with higher baseline biomarker levels. Elevated baseline CCL18 predicted FVC deterioration in unadjusted analysis, and higher baseline CCL18 and KL-6 were independently associated with disease progression after adjusting for age, sex, and baseline FVC. Baseline CA-125 was associated with FVC deterioration after adjustment, and its relative changes over 6 months were associated with FVC deterioration and showed a trend toward disease progression. When comparing predictive models, individual biomarkers showed discriminative performance comparable to clinical variables, and their addition to clinical variables resulted in a slight, non-significant improvement in performance (area under the curve for FVC deterioration increasing from 0.769 to 0.824).
CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that several blood biomarkers, particularly CCL18, KL-6, and CA-125, may provide additional prognostic information for IPF patients receiving pirfenidone and warrant further investigation.

candidates.title: Beyond the Lungs: A Case of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Cutaneous Sarcoidosis Without Pulmonary Involvement.
candidates.journal: Journal of investigative medicine high impact case reports
candidates.abstract: The coexistence of sarcoidosis and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an uncommon but increasingly recognized phenomenon. Limited data exist regarding its epidemiology, clinical manifestations, and optimal management. We present the case of a 58-year-old female with a history of SLE who developed a chronic, relapsing annular rash affecting her arms and neck over three years. She also experienced frequent headaches with normal neuroimaging. Laboratory testing revealed positive antinuclear antibody (ANA), anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA), Cytoplasmic Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody (C-ANCA) with Anti-Proteinase 3 (PR3) specificity, nucleosome antibodies. A skin biopsy subsequently led to a diagnosis of cutaneous sarcoidosis. Unlike most reported cases, which primarily feature pulmonary involvement, this patient exhibited no significant respiratory symptoms. The unusual presence of C-ANCA positivity, more commonly associated with vasculitis, raised the possibility of an overlap syndrome. She was successfully treated with corticosteroids and hydroxychloroquine, resulting in clinical improvement. This case highlights the need to consider cutaneous sarcoidosis as a potential coexisting condition with SLE, particularly in the absence of pulmonary involvement. Increased awareness of atypical presentations may lead to earlier recognition and improved outcomes. Further research is warranted to better characterize the relationship between these two autoimmune conditions and to refine therapeutic strategies for patients with this rare coexistence.

candidates.title: Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita in a Patient With Sarcoidosis.
candidates.abstract: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) is a rare auto- immune subepidermal blistering disease targeting type VII collagen at the dermal-epidermal junction. Although EBA is associated with several systemic diseases, its coexistence with sarcoidosis is exceedingly rare. We describe a 57-year-old woman with long-standing pulmonary sarcoidosis who developed a progressive blistering eruption of the extremities and groin with oral discomfort, burning pain, and pruritus. Biopsy showed a subepidermal blister with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, and direct immunofluorescence demonstrated linear IgA, IgG, and IgM deposition along the basement membrane zone. Our clinicopathologic findings favored inflammatory-type EBA. Treatment with oral and topical corticosteroids, and subsequently oral dapsone, achieved resolution of blistering with minimal scarring. This case highlights the importance of recognizing inflamma- tory EBA and expands the limited literature describing coexistent EBA and sarcoidosis.

candidates.title: Chronic ulcerative colitis complicated by granulomatosis with polyangiitis and late-onset rectal cancer: A case report.
candidates.abstract:
RATIONALE: Ulcerative colitis (UC) and granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) are distinct autoimmune disorders, and their coexistence is rarely reported. Furthermore, long-term malignant complications in patients with both conditions have been infrequently described. Consequently, long-term management strategies and surveillance for intestinal cancer risk in patients with concomitant UC and GPA remain poorly defined.
PATIENT CONCERNS: A male patient initially diagnosed with extensive UC sequentially developed sacroiliitis and subsequently GPA during a 13-year disease course, confirmed by renal and cutaneous involvement.
DIAGNOSES: The patient was diagnosed with long-standing extensive ulcerative colitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, sigmoid colon adenocarcinoma, and rectal adenocarcinoma.
INTERVENTIONS: The patient received long-term maintenance therapy with glucocorticoids and underwent laparoscopic radical rectal cancer resection combined with total colectomy and permanent ileostomy, followed by adjuvant XELOX (oxaliplatin plus capecitabine) chemotherapy.
OUTCOMES: The patient tolerated the chemotherapy well, with only grade 1 gastrointestinal adverse events and no severe myelosuppression. He is currently undergoing regular adjuvant chemotherapy and continues standardized multidisciplinary long-term outpatient surveillance.
LESSONS: This case highlights the cumulative risk of concurrent autoimmune comorbidities and malignant transformation in long-standing UC, while emphasizing the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges associated with multisystem overlapping inflammatory disorders. It also adds to the limited body of literature describing the coexistence of inflammatory bowel disease, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis, and rectal adenocarcinoma.

candidates.title: Reduced HRCT-Derived T4-Level Pectoralis Muscle Volume in Connective Tissue Disease Associated Interstitial Lung Disease: An Exploratory Case Control Study.
candidates.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: To evaluate whether high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT)-derived T4-level single-slice segmented total pectoralis muscle volume (PecToT) differs between connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (CTD-ILD) patients and non-CTD non-ILD controls, and whether it reflects fibrotic disease burden or thoracic muscle quantity.
METHODS: In this single-center cross-sectional case-control study, 50 CTD-ILD patients and 48 non-CTD non-ILD HRCT controls underwent HRCT-based pectoral muscle assessment at the mid-T4 level. PecToT was defined as the sum of bilateral pectoralis major and minor segmented volumes within -29 to +150 HU. Low PecToT was defined using sex-specific 25th percentile thresholds derived from controls. Multivariable regression, receiver operating characteristic analysis, model performance comparisons, and exploratory fibrosis-dominant HRCT burden analyses were performed.
RESULTS: PecToT was significantly lower in CTD-ILD patients than controls (median 0.8836 vs. 1.3530, p < 0.001). CTD-ILD versus non-CTD non-ILD HRCT control status remained independently associated with lower PecToT after adjustment for age, sex, BMI, and smoking (B = -0.480, 95% CI -0.671 to -0.290, p < 0.001). PecToT discriminated CTD-ILD from controls with good performance (AUC = 0.802, 95% CI 0.710-0.887; cut-off 1.058; sensitivity 72.0%, specificity 81.3%). Adding PecToT to clinical variables improved AUC from 0.668 to 0.846. Low PecToT was present in 84.0% of CTD-ILD patients and remained strongly associated with CTD-ILD versus non-CTD non-ILD HRCT control status (OR = 22.62, 95% CI 6.80-75.19, p < 0.001). PecToT did not correlate with Warrick score, FVC, DLCO, CRP, ESR, or fibrosis-dominant HRCT burden. Interobserver reliability was excellent (ICC = 0.92).
CONCLUSION: HRCT-derived PecToT reproducibly distinguished CTD-ILD patients from non-CTD non-ILD controls and appeared to reflect reduced thoracic muscle quantity rather than fibrotic severity.

candidates.title: Effect of Nerandomilast in US Patients with Progressive Pulmonary Fibrosis: A Subgroup Analysis of the FIBRONEER-ILD Trial.
candidates.abstract:
PURPOSE: In the FIBRONEER-ILD trial in patients with progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF), nerandomilast reduced decline in forced vital capacity (FVC) versus placebo, with benefits on clinical outcomes and favorable safety and tolerability. We present the effects of nerandomilast in US patients.
METHODS: Patients were randomized to receive nerandomilast 9 mg bid, nerandomilast 18 mg bid, or placebo, stratified by nintedanib use and HRCT pattern. In the US subgroup, we assessed change in FVC (mL) at week 52; time-to-event endpoints over the whole trial; and adverse events over the whole trial.
RESULTS: Of 1176 patients, 139 (11.8%) were from the US. In the US patients, adjusted mean (SE) changes in FVC (mL) at week 52 were - 160.4 (35.7) with placebo, - 115.2 (38.6) with nerandomilast 9 mg bid (difference vs. placebo 45.2 [95% CI: -57.8, 148.2]), and - 53.4 (37.3) with nerandomilast 18 mg bid (difference vs. placebo 107.0 [95% CI: 6.2, 207.9]). The hazard ratios (95% CI) for time to first acute exacerbation of ILD, hospitalization for respiratory cause, or death were 0.88 (0.42, 1.81) for nerandomilast 9 mg bid and 0.52 (0.23, 1.18) for nerandomilast 18 mg bid versus placebo. Adverse events led to treatment discontinuation in 14.0, 11.4 and 8.9% of the placebo, nerandomilast 9 mg bid and nerandomilast 18 mg bid groups, respectively.
CONCLUSION: In the FIBRONEER-ILD trial, the effects of nerandomilast in US patients were consistent with the overall population, with a reduction in FVC decline, numerically reduced risk of adverse clinical outcomes, and favorable safety and tolerability.

candidates.title: Effect of Nerandomilast in US Patients with Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis: a Subgroup Analysis of the FIBRONEER-IPF Trial.
candidates.abstract:
PURPOSE: In the placebo-controlled FIBRONEER-IPF trial in patients with IPF, nerandomilast reduced decline in forced vital capacity (FVC), with benefits on clinical outcomes and favorable safety and tolerability. We evaluated the effects of nerandomilast in the US patients.
METHODS: Patients were randomized to receive nerandomilast 9 mg bid, nerandomilast 18 mg bid, or placebo, stratified by antifibrotic therapy (nintedanib/pirfenidone versus neither). In the US subgroup, we assessed change in FVC at week 52; time-to-event endpoints over the whole trial; adverse events over the whole trial.
RESULTS: Of 1177 patients, 196 (16.7%) were from the US. In US patients, adjusted mean (SE) changes in FVC (mL) were - 257.9 (33.6) with placebo, - 152.7 (32.9) with nerandomilast 9 mg bid (difference vs. placebo 105.2 [95% CI 13.0, 197.4]), and - 126.2 (36.9) with nerandomilast 18 mg bid (difference vs. placebo 131.7 [95% CI 33.8, 229.6]. Compared with placebo, the hazard ratios for time to first acute exacerbation of IPF, hospitalization for respiratory cause, or death were 0.91 (95% CI 0.49, 1.67) for nerandomilast 9 mg bid and 0.60 (95% CI 0.30, 1.22) for nerandomilast 18 mg bid. Adverse events led to treatment discontinuation in 17.1%, 12.9% and 10.7% of the placebo, nerandomilast 9 mg bid and nerandomilast 18 mg bid groups, respectively.
CONCLUSION: The effects of nerandomilast 18 mg bid in US patients in the FIBRONEER-IPF trial were consistent with the overall population. Nerandomilast 18 mg bid slowed FVC decline, with numerical reductions in the risk of clinical outcomes, and favorable safety and tolerability.

candidates.title: Mesenchymal Stem Cells for Interstitial Lung Disease: A Review of Mechanisms, Clinical Evidence, and Subtype-Specific Outcomes.
candidates.abstract: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) encompasses a heterogeneous group of progressive pulmonary disorders driven by persistent alveolar injury, chronic inflammation, and aberrant fibrosis. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have emerged as a promising cell therapy due to their immunomodulatory, anti-fibrosis, and pro-regenerative properties, which have been demonstrated by nonclinical studies. Clinical trials mainly focused on idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and systemic sclerosis - associated ILD (SSc-ILD) showed a favorable safety profile with only transient mild adverse events. As for effectiveness, early phase studies suggest that MSCs can stabilize forced vital capacity and diffusing capacity of IPF patients, which is a possible signal of disease stabilization. In SSc-ILD, lung function and imaging improvement have been reported in some studies. Although these observations derive from small numbers of SSc-ILD patients within broader SSc cohorts and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than comparative evidence. While efficacy remains to be confirmed in larger randomized trials. Persistent challenges include donor heterogeneity, optimal dosing, route selection, and manufacturing scalability. Collectively, MSCs offer a safe and promising but still investigational disease-modifying candidate for ILD, although their therapeutic potential remains constrained by disease subtype and the irreversibility of established fibrosis.

candidates.title: Pirfenidone Induced Photosensitive Rash in Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis.
candidates.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a gradually worsening interstitial lung disease ordinarily managed with anti-fibrotic agents such as pirfenidone, which has been shown to slow the disease progression but may be linked with adverse effects such as gastrointestinal intolerance and cutaneous reactions. Awareness of photosensitivity as a potential side effect is essential to ensure treatment adherence as well as patient safety. We report the case of a 63-year-old gentleman with moderately severe IPF who was started on oral pirfenidone and consequently developed a widespread erythematous rash within one month, initially affecting sun-exposed areas before becoming more generalised. Dermatological assessment suggested a photosensitive reaction, and the patient was acknowledged as lack of awareness regarding sun-protection measures. Pirfenidone was quickly discontinued, and he was started on oral and topical corticosteroids alongside counselling on strict sun protection. Skin biopsy was performed and histopathological findings were persistent with photosensitive dermatitis. The rash resolved gradually over two to three weeks without residual changes, and there was no recurrence on followup with continuous adherence to sun-protective measures. This case highlights the importance of being familiar with pirfenidone-induced photosensitivity and highlighting preventive advice when initiating therapy.

candidates.title: GMP manufacturing, quality characterization, and GLP-based preclinical evaluation of human nasal turbinate-derived stem cells for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Human nasal turbinate-derived stem cells (hNTSCs) are tissue-derived adult stem cells that are isolated from surgically discarded nasal turbinate tissue and exhibit robust proliferative capacity, and stable phenotypic properties. Unlike conventional MSCs, hNTSCs, although classified as tissue-derived adult stem cells, exhibit MSC-like phenotypes but display distinct gene expression patterns and functional properties that may be advantageous for indications of inflammatory and autoimmune disease. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by persistent synovitis, progressive joint destruction, and incomplete responses to existing disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs and biologics. Cell-based immunomodulatory therapies represent promising alternative strategies; however, the clinical translation of novel stem cell platforms requires not only the demonstration of therapeutic efficacy but also establishment of a reproducible manufacturing process, rigorous quality characterization, and comprehensive nonclinical safety evaluation.In this study, we developed a clinical-grade injectable hNTSC product for treating RA by integrating a GMP-equivalent manufacturing process, systematic quality control (QC) testing, and GLP-compliant nonclinical safety, biodistribution, and efficacy assessments. This integrated regulatory science framework supports the potential of hNTSCs as a distinct and clinically translatable adult stem cell platform for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis.
METHODS: Clinical-grade hNTSCs were manufactured from surgically obtained nasal turbinate tissue using a GMP-equivalent process that included serial cell expansion, multitiered cell banking, and final drug product formulation. candidates.title: Association between quantitative computed tomography metrics and pulmonary function in patients with post-COVID-19 pulmonary fibrosis: a single-center cross-sectional study.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Post-COVID-19 pulmonary fibrosis is an important long-term complication of severe SARS-CoV-2 infection. Quantitative computed tomography (QCT) provides observer-independent measurement of parenchymal abnormality. However, the association between structural lung abnormalities and functional impairment remains insufficiently characterized. We quantified the cross-sectional association between a CT-derived density metric and pulmonary function, exercise capacity and dyspnea.
METHODS: Single-center cross-sectional study of 39 adults assessed approximately one year after severe COVID-19 pneumonia; each underwent one chest CT and one pulmonary function assessment, with no serial imaging or serial physiology. QCT was performed in 3D Slicer v5.0.3 with the Lung CT Analyzer extension. Collapse percentage (collapse%) was defined as the volume of intrapulmonary tissue with attenuation above - 400 HU, after exclusion of vessels (> 0 HU), divided by total lung volume (TLV) - the non-aerated compartment of the established CT aeration model. Spirometry followed the 2019 ATS/ERS standards; exercise capacity was assessed by 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) with Borg dyspnea scoring. Correlation coefficients are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) was unavailable.

candidates.title: Pulmonary function trajectories in non-UIP ANCA-positive idiopathic interstitial pneumonia under real-world treatment.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-positive idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (ANCA-IIP) is an interstitial lung disease (ILD) phenotype with ANCA seropositivity but no systemic evidence of vasculitis, and its disease position and treatment strategy remain uncertain. Patients with non-usual interstitial pneumonia (non-UIP) ANCA-IIP are frequently treated with glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive agents in clinical practice. However, previous studies have mainly focused on clinical characteristics and prognosis, while longitudinal changes in pulmonary function under real-world treatment conditions remain insufficiently described. This study aimed to address the following research question: among patients with ANCA-positive interstitial lung disease (ANCA-ILD), how do pulmonary function trajectories in patients with non-UIP ANCA-IIP differ from those in patients with microscopic polyangiitis-associated interstitial lung disease (MPA-ILD)?
METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort study screened 1,024 patients with ILD and available ANCA testing between January 2012 and January 2022. Patients with non-UIP ANCA-IIP and MPA-ILD were included according to final multidisciplinary diagnosis and high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) pattern. Locally weighted scatterplot smoothing with bootstrap 95% CIs was used to visualize 36-month trajectories of forced expiratory volume in 1 s, forced vital capacity (FVC), total lung capacity, diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DLCO), and prednisone-equivalent dose. Segmented linear mixed-effects models with a 12-month knot compared pulmonary function slopes during 0 to 12 months and 12 to 36 months.

candidates.title: A multiparametric nomogram to reduce unnecessary EBUS-TBNA in suspected lung cancer: development and internal validation in an anthracosis-prevalent cohort.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) is the first-line invasive modality for evaluating mediastinal lymphadenopathy in suspected lung cancer, yet it entails sedation, cost, and non-diagnostic results. In regions with a high prevalence of anthracosis, 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18 F-FDG PET/CT) specificity is reduced because pigmented and granulomatous nodes produce 18 F-FDG-avid benign lymphadenopathy mimicking malignancy. We developed and internally validated a multiparametric nomogram to support pre-procedural triage and reduce unnecessary EBUS-TBNA referrals.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective study analyzed 337 consecutive adults who underwent EBUS-TBNA between January 2019 and November 2025 (184 malignant, 153 benign by cytopathology). For each patient, an index node was defined as the station-level node with the highest SUVmax and largest short-axis diameter. Mean Hounsfield unit (HU) and SUVmax were measured by two blinded readers (intraclass correlation coefficients 0.95 and 0.93). Multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors. Discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility were assessed by area under the curve (AUC), Hosmer-Lemeshow testing with calibration slope, and decision curve analysis. Internal validation used 1,000-iteration bootstrap optimism correction. Sex-specific decision thresholds were derived under a pre-specified false-negative-rate constraint of ≤ 5%.
RESULTS: Five independent predictors were retained: female sex (adjusted odds ratio 0.29, 95% confidence interval 0.17-0.49), age ≥ 65 years (0.42, 0.25-0.70), short-axis diameter (1.05/mm, 1.02-1.10), mean HU (0.988/unit, 0.978-0.999), and SUVmax (1.16/unit, 1.09-1.23). candidates.fulltext: IntroductionLung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and accurate mediastinal staging is essential for treatment selection [1]. In patients with suspected lung cancer who present with mediastinal lymphadenopathy on chest computed tomography (CT) or 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (18 F-FDG PET/CT), endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) is the first-line invasive modality for tissue diagnosis [1–3]. EBUS-TBNA has high diagnostic yield and low morbidity, yet the procedure entails moderate sedation, procedural cost, and a non-trivial rate of non-diagnostic results [2, 3]. When a meaningful proportion of patients referred for EBUS-TBNA ultimately have benign disease, unnecessary invasive sampling delays appropriate management and consumes interventional pulmonology resources. Selective referral, supported by accurate non-invasive triage, is therefore desirable.The non-invasive imaging tools used for triage have well-known specificity limitations. PET/CT exhibits high sensitivity but specificity that frequently falls below 65% in heterogeneous populations [4, 5]. False-positive 18 F-FDG uptake is particularly common where granulomatous and dust-related processes are prevalent, because inflammatory and reactive nodes produce SUVmax values that overlap substantially with those of metastatic disease [4, 5]. Anthracosis and anthracofibrosis — pigmented benign nodal processes associated with long-term exposure to inhaled particulates including biomass smoke, coal dust, and air pollution — are recognized causes of 18 F-FDG-avid benign lymphadenopathy that mimics malignancy [5]. In regions where these processes are common, PET-based triage alone may prompt invasive sampling in patients with a low pre-test probability of malignancy.This diagnostic challenge is particularly relevant in tuberculosis-endemic regions of central Anatolia, where anthracotic mediastinal lymphadenopathy is a frequent referral finding [6–8]. Quantitative CT measurements, particularly mean Hounsfield unit (HU) values of mediastinal lymph nodes, have been proposed as adjunctive markers because benign nodes tend to display higher attenuation than metastatic ones [9]. Used in isolation, however, both HU and SUVmax show only moderate discriminative ability, and their combined use with demographic and anatomical predictors has not been adequately studied in this clinical setting [9, 10]. Recent nomogram-based approaches integrating sonographic, demographic, and metabolic variables have improved performance in selected cohorts [10–19], but most published models predict lymph node metastasis in patients with already-confirmed lung cancer [20]. Earlier work has attempted to separate benign from malignant nodes using CT attenuation alone. Our contribution is the integration of quantitative CT HU values and PET SUVmax, tailored to a specific epidemiological background: a region with a high prevalence of anthracosis, where isolated PET evaluation yields a very high false-positive rate. It targets the failure of PET-based triage in that setting, not the generic benign-versus-malignant question.We developed and internally validated a multiparametric nomogram for pre-procedural triage of mediastinal lymphadenopathy in patients with suspected lung cancer in an anthracosis-prevalent cohort. The model integrates five routinely available demographic and imaging (CT and PET) variables to estimate malignancy probability before EBUS-TBNA, with the explicit goal of reducing unnecessary invasive referrals while preserving high sensitivity for malignancy. We quantified the model’s incremental value over standalone PET-based assessment, derived sex-specific decision thresholds under a pre-specified false-negative-rate constraint, and examined performance in a pre-specified anthracosis-versus-malignancy subgroup. We present this study in accordance with the TRIPOD reporting checklist [21].MethodsStudy designThis single-center retrospective study at Necmettin Erbakan University, Faculty of Medicine (Konya, Türkiye) was conducted in accordance with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its subsequent amendments. The Necmettin Erbakan University Non-Drug and Medical Device Research Ethics Committee approved the protocol (No: 2025/6238; 26 December 2025) and waived the requirement for individual informed consent for this retrospective analysis. Reporting followed the TRIPOD guideline [21] (Online Resource 1).Patient selectionConsecutive adults (≥ 18 years) who underwent EBUS-TBNA for mediastinal lymphadenopathy between 1 January 2019 and 1 November 2025 were screened. candidates.title: NGF-TRKA Facilitates the Activation of Lung Fibroblasts and Modulates the Immune Response in Pulmonary Fibrosis Via the FAK/ERK Signaling Pathway.
candidates.abstract: A growing body of evidence suggests that immune dysregulation plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF); however, the precise regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. We aim to identify key inflammatory factors and immune cells that significantly contribute to the onset and progression of IPF, and to elucidate their specific mechanisms of action. The potential causal relationships between 731 immunocyte phenotype, 41 inflammatory cytokines and IPF were conducted using bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (TwoSampleMR) analysis. The candidate targets were further screened in the peripheral blood of patients with IPF, as well as in both in vivo and in vitro models of pulmonary fibrosis (PF). In vitro experiments were performed by treating MRC5 cells with nerve growth factor (NGF) and the tropomyosin receptor kinase A (TRKA) inhibitor K-252a, or by transfecting the cells with siRNA targeting TRKA. Fibroblast activation was assessed using CCK-8 assays, wound healing assays, transwell migration assays, reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), and western blot analysis. Additionally, co-immunoprecipitation (CoIP) was employed to verify the interaction between NGF and TRKA in MRC5 cells. In vivo studies examined the impact of NGF on immune responses and PF, as well as the antifibrotic effects of K-252a on these parameters. These evaluations were performed through histopathological examination, immunohistochemical analysis, immunofluorescence analysis, western blotting, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). The genetically predicted onset of IPF has been correlated with the expression of NGF, which is significantly upregulated in the peripheral blood of individuals diagnosed with IPF. candidates.fulltext: Introduction Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic and progressive lung disease that affects the interstitial tissue, showing an usual interstitial pneumonia pattern detected through high-resolution computed tomography or biopsy with no identifiable cause [1]. In Europe and North America, the incidence of IPF varies from 3 to 9 cases per 100,000 individuals per year, with a yearly rise in numbers [2]. The outlook for IPF is grim, with a median survival of just 3–5 years post-diagnosis, which is less promising than the prognosis for many cancer types [3]. Early identification or intervention of IPF is crucial for improving outcomes given the restricted treatment options currently available, primarily consisting of anti-fibrotic drugs that offer only modest reduction in the rate of lung function decline over the course of the disease [4]. Although there is a significant correlation between the recurrent injury to epithelial cells and the stimulation of lung fibroblasts activation in the progression of IPF [5], the precise pathogenic mechanisms remain incompletely elucidated. Therefore, gaining a comprehensive understanding of the pathogenesis of IPF would facilitate the development of more effective and safer therapeutic interventions.Several hypotheses have been proposed to explain the specific etiology of IPF to date. However, a growing body of evidence suggests that the progression of IPF is markedly impacted by both innate and adaptive immune responses [6, 7]. While initial assumptions regarding the significance of inflammation in IPF have been challenged owing to the lack of efficacy of anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive therapies in improving lung function and survival [8], this finding itself does not negate the potential immune-mediated nature of the disease. Alternatively, these clinical failures indicate that the choice of specific immunomodulatory therapy in previous trials may have been inappropriate. Indeed, a review by Shenderov et al. [9], drawing on evidence from human and murine studies reported in the past decade, underscores the pivotal role of immune dysregulation in driving the progression of IPF. However, the precise influence of the immune system on the progression and onset of the IPF remains uncertain, potentially due to limited sample sizes, methodological inaccuracies, and uncontrolled variables in contemporary studies. Therefore, further investigations are warranted to clarify the causal relationship between the immune system and IPF.Investigations into the involvement of the immune system in IPF have revealed novel opportunities for therapeutic intervention, particularly those guided by genetic insights. Prior large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified several immune cell populations and inflammatory cytokines that may be implicated in IPF pathogenesis [10–14]. However, a thorough understanding of the complex biological pathways connecting immune cells and inflammatory mediators remains incomplete. Furthermore, existing research has yet to definitively establish the specific roles of immune cells or inflammatory factors in the development of IPF, nor has it comprehensively elucidated the underlying mechanisms. To address these gaps, a bidirectional Two-Sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis was conducted to assess the potential contribution of the immune system to IPF progression, with particular emphasis on immune cell subsets and inflammatory cytokines. The results identified nerve growth factor (NGF) as a critical inflammatory mediator significantly associated with IPF onset, alongside two immune cell types, notably CD4 on CD39+ regulatory T (Treg) cells.NGF, a neurotrophin family member, is essential for regulating neuronal growth and survival. It acts as an extracellular ligand for the p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR) and tropomyosin receptor kinase A (TRKA), thereby initiating cellular signaling cascades that govern neuronal proliferation, differentiation, and survival [15]. Although previous studies have linked NGF and p75NTR to liver fibrosis [16], research exploring their roles in pulmonary fibrosis (PF) and the specific mechanisms involved remain limited. NGF has been shown to promote proliferation and migration of triple-negative breast cancer cells by inducing the assembly of a TrkA/β1-integrin/Focal adhesion kinase (FAK)/Src complex [17]. In the context of pulmonary fibrosis, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress has been reported to facilitate the proliferation of lung fibroblasts [18]. Additionally, TrkA has been implicated in modulating the transcriptional regulation of ER stress-related genes in human neuronal cells [19]. Phosphorylation-dependent activation of B lymphoid tyrosine kinase (BLK) requires its interaction with FAK to form a complex, which subsequently exacerbates endometrial fibrosis through the regulation of ER stress [20]. candidates.title: Factors Associated With Radiation Pneumonitis and Prognosis in Esophageal Cancer Patients Undergoing Radiotherapy.
candidates.journal: Cancer control : journal of the Moffitt Cancer Center
candidates.abstract: IntroductionRadiation-induced lung injury (RILI) is one of the most severe complications in esophageal cancer (EC) patients undergoing radiotherapy. However, the risk factors for acute radiation pneumonitis (RP) have not been fully clarified. This study aimed to explore the factors associated to RP induced by precise radiotherapy and the prognosis of EC patients.MethodsThis single-center retrospective observational study enrolled 101 EC patients who underwent radiotherapy for primary lesions and/or mediastinal metastatic lymph nodes. The relationships between clinical characteristics, dosimetric parameters, hematological markers of inflammation, and the occurrence of RP were analyzed. The cutoff values were determined by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Multivariable logistic regression and Kaplan-Meier methods were also performed to investigate the prognostic role of these factors.ResultsThe incidence rate of RP in this study was 47.52%, but most cases (75%) suffered grade 1 RP. Univariate analysis indicated that neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), systemic immune-inflammatory index (SII), system inflammation response index (SIRI), V5, V10, V15, V20, V25, V30, and lung mean dose (Dmean) affected the occurrence of RP. Multivariate logistic regression analysis identified SII, SIRI, and V20 as independent risk factors for RP in EC patients. The area under the curve (AUC) of the combined model was 0.83 (95% CI, 0.752-0.909, P < 0.05), yielding a higher predictive accuracy. Further analysis indicated that elevated pretreatment SII and SIRI were related with poor prognosis in EC patients.ConclusionsThis study demonstrated that SII, SIRI, and V20 are potential independent predictors of RP in EC. Patients with high SII and SIRI have shorter survival. Further investigation combining multiple features for predicting RP in EC patients and its impact on patient prognosis is warranted.

candidates.title: Anamorelin in patients with idiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis: A prospective, single-arm, open-label pilot study.
candidates.abstract: BackgroundIdiopathic pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis (iPPFE) is a rare, progressive interstitial lung disease with a poor prognosis and no established pharmacological treatment. Cachexia and cachexia-related symptoms are common in patients with iPPFE and are associated with functional decline and poor outcomes.ObjectivesTo evaluate the efficacy and safety of anamorelin, an oral ghrelin receptor agonist, in patients with iPPFE.DesignProspective interventional study.MethodsIn this single-arm pilot study, patients with iPPFE received oral anamorelin hydrochloride (100 mg once daily) for 8 weeks. The primary endpoint was the change in anorexia- and cachexia-related symptoms assessed using the Anorexia/Cachexia Subscale of the Functional Assessment of Anorexia/Cachexia Therapy (FAACT-A/CS). Exploratory endpoints included changes in body weight, lean body mass, nutritional biomarkers, dyspnoea severity, respiratory-related quality of life (QOL), and handgrip strength. Safety was assessed through clinical and laboratory evaluations.ResultsNineteen patients were enrolled; 18 received at least one dose of anamorelin, and 15 were included in the efficacy analyses. The median FAACT-A/CS score increased from 26 to 36, with a Hodges-Lehmann estimate of 5.0 (95% confidence interval, 0.5-9.5) (p = 0.028). Body weight, lean body mass, prealbumin, and transferrin levels increased from baseline. Circulating growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) levels also increased. Dyspnoea severity decreased, respiratory-related QOL scores increased, and handgrip strength increased. No treatment-related serious adverse events occurred; however, two participants discontinued treatment because of treatment-related adverse events (hepatic enzyme elevation and generalised oedema).ConclusionTreatment with anamorelin was associated with improvements in cachexia-related symptoms, body weight, body composition, nutritional biomarkers, respiratory-related QOL, and pharmacodynamic ef

candidates.title: Identification and monitoring of immune-related adverse reactions of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors based on symptom network analysis.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors have become first-line cancer therapies by disrupting immune checkpoint downregulation, thereby potentiating antitumor immunity. However, this enhanced immune activation may also target normal tissues, triggering multisystemic immune-related adverse events (irAE) that complicate clinical management. Conventional pharmacovigilance analyses typically assess individual adverse events in isolation, limiting the ability to capture inter-symptom relationships. Symptom network analysis, an emerging computational approach, constructs co-occurrence networks to identify core symptoms, key associations, and bridge nodes across organ systems, thus enabling a systematic understanding of complex suspected irAE profiles.
METHODS: Adverse event records for six PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors were extracted from two spontaneous reporting databases: FAERS (Q1 2005-Q3 2024) and JADER (Q1 2004-Q1 2025). Potential signals were screened using reporting odds ratio(ROR), proportional reporting ratio(PRR), and multivariate gamma-Poisson shrinkage (MGPS) methods. Symptom co-occurrence networks were subsequently constructed using EBIC-GLASSO based on Tetrachoric correlation matrices, which are specifically designed for binary adverse event data and correct for attenuation due to dichotomization. Four centrality metrics-Strength, Closeness, Betweenness, and Expected Influence-were calculated via the qgraph package. The bootnet package performed 1,000 bootstrap iterations to evaluate 95% confidence intervals for edge weights and centrality stability coefficients.
RESULTS: In FAERS, nivolumab (48,330) and pembrolizumab (37,224) generated the highest report volumes. PD-1 inhibitor networks consistently centered on a systemic-gastrointestinal symptom cluster comprising decreased appetite, fatigue, diarrhea, and nausea, whereas PD-L1 inhibitor networks additionally featured prominent hematologic abnormalities. candidates.fulltext: 1IntroductionImmune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) enhance the body’s immune response against tumor cells by precisely targeting and inhibiting immune checkpoints, thereby achieving therapeutic efficacy and establishing a novel paradigm in cancer treatment (1). ICIs comprise a variety of agents targeting distinct molecules. Among these, programmed cell death receptor-1 (PD-1) and programmed death-ligand-1 (PD-L1) inhibitors have delivered significant breakthroughs and emerged as first-line therapeutic agents (2). Compared to conventional cancer therapies, PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors harness the patient’s own immune system to eliminate tumor cells and are considered a more effective modality for managing recurrent and metastatic cancers (3). While these agents yield excellent therapeutic outcomes, they are also associated with a spectrum of adverse drug reactions. Immune-related adverse events (irAE) (4) may arise when the immune system becomes dysregulated and targets healthy tissues, potentially affecting multiple organ systems. Common adverse events involve the gastrointestinal tract, endocrine system, and thyroid gland (5); severe cases may necessitate treatment discontinuation.Symptom network analysis offers a comprehensive approach to examining disease-related symptoms in patients, quantitatively assessing the associations between different symptoms through complex network analysis (6). In this study, we employed symptom network analysis to investigate irAE associated with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor use reported in the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) and the Japanese Adverse Drug Event Reporting System (JADER) databases. This study examines the network structure, nodes, and metrics of adverse reaction symptoms to elucidate the relationships among these symptoms in real-world settings and to explore the potential mechanisms underlying symptom clusters. The findings aim to provide a reference for the safe clinical use of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors and for the timely detection and management of irAE.Unlike conventional pharmacovigilance methods—such as disproportionality analysis (e.g., ROR, PRR)—which assess individual adverse events in isolation and merely identify statistically over-represented drug-event pairs, symptom network analysis offers a fundamentally different perspective. Rather than examining single adverse events independently, this approach models the co-occurrence patterns among symptoms, revealing how different suspected irAE are interconnected within and across organ systems. This enables the identification of core symptom clusters, bridging symptoms that connect multiple systems, and structurally central nodes that may represent clinically important indicators of widespread symptom co-occurrence. Thus, while disproportionality analysis answers “which adverse events are statistically associated with a drug”, symptom network analysis addresses the more clinically relevant question: “how do these adverse events relate to each other, and which symptoms play the most central role in the overall irAE landscape?”In this study, we identified potential irAE signals using MedDRA Preferred Terms (PTs) that have been previously reported as immune-related in clinical trials and pharmacovigilance studies. These terms represent only suspected irAE recorded in spontaneous reporting databases, rather than clinically confirmed irAE following comprehensive clinical assessment. Throughout this manuscript, we therefore use the term “suspected irAE” to refer to these reported events.2Materials and methods2.1Study design and data sourcesThis study extracted and processed adverse reaction data for PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors from the FAERS database (covering Q1–2005 through Q3 2024) and the JADER database (covering January 2004 through January 2025).The FAERS database is a repository of spontaneous adverse drug reaction reports submitted by pharmaceutical companies, healthcare professionals, and consumers. It contains a substantial volume of publicly available adverse event reports and supports the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in monitoring adverse reactions to approved drugs and biological products (7). Each Standard Information Exchange Code (SIEC) file in this dataset is divided into seven distinct sections: patient demographics and administrative details, drug information, adverse events, patient outcomes, reporting source, start and end dates of drug therapy, and indications for use or diagnosis. Within the database framework, these files are linked via unique identifiers such as PRIMARYID. Data from the FAERS database were extracted using OpenVigil 2.1 (https://openvigil.sourceforge.net/) (8), a platform that standardizes FAERS data according to FDA processing standards. OpenVigil 2.1 initially performed deduplication by retaining unique reports based on Individual Safety Report (ISR) identifiers, which yielded 111,542 cases. candidates.title: Risk stratification for immune-related pneumonitis in esophageal cancer: differential roles of systemic inflammation across severity grades and additive effect of radiation.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibition is increasingly integrated with thoracic radiotherapy in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), but checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis (CIP) remains a clinically important toxicity. Whether baseline systemic inflammation modifies the association between lung radiation dose and clinically significant CIP is unclear.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort included 268 patients with ESCC treated with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors; 154 subsequently received thoracic radiotherapy. Baseline systemic inflammation was assessed using the systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) from a complete blood count obtained within 7 days before the first immunotherapy dose. The primary endpoint was grade ≥2 CIP according to CTCAE v5.0; grade ≥1 and grade ≥3 CIP were secondary endpoints. Multivariable Cox models evaluated clinical risk factors, and SII-by-V20 interaction analyses were performed in the radiotherapy subgroup. The grade ≥2 nomogram underwent 10-fold cross-validation, 1,000-resample bootstrap validation/calibration, and decision-curve analysis.
RESULTS: In the overall cohort, 77/268 (28.7%), 29/268 (10.8%), and 19/268 (7.1%) patients developed grade ≥1, grade ≥2, and grade ≥3 CIP, respectively. In the radiotherapy subgroup, the corresponding event counts were 54/154 (35.1%), 20/154 (13.0%), and 13/154 (8.4%). High SII, thoracic radiotherapy, and COPD were independently associated with CIP, while higher BMI was protective. The association of V20 with CIP was concentrated in the high-SII subgroup, with significant SII×V20 interactions across severity thresholds. The nomogram had a C-index of 0.758 (95% CI, 0.680-0.836); the mean 10-fold cross-validated C-index was 0.74 (95% CI, 0.69-0.79), and the bootstrap optimism-corrected C-index was 0.73. Calibration and decision-curve analyses supported acceptable internal performance and potential clinical utility.

candidates.fulltext: IntroductionImmune checkpoint inhibitors are increasingly incorporated into multimodality treatment for esophageal cancer, while thoracic radiotherapy remains an important component of active local-control strategies in appropriately selected patients (1). Checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis (CIP) is a clinically important cause of morbidity and treatment interruption (2, 3). Its management is complicated by overlap with other causes of pneumonitis and by substantial heterogeneity in severity (4, 5). Some patients experience only mild radiographic abnormalities, whereas others develop symptomatic or severe pneumonitis (6, 7).Current CIP risk prediction remains limited (8, 9). Radiation dosimetry, including lung V20 and mean lung dose (MLD), has been studied in relation to treatment-related pulmonary toxicity (10, 11). Separately, pretreatment inflammatory markers such as SII have been investigated as markers of immune-related and oncologic outcomes (12). Whether the association between radiation dose and CIP differs according to baseline systemic inflammatory status remains incompletely defined.We therefore conducted a retrospective cohort study with two complementary analyses. First, we evaluated baseline SII and clinical factors associated with CIP in the overall immunotherapy-treated cohort. Second, among patients who received thoracic radiotherapy, we examined the association between lung V20 and CIP within SII strata and formally tested the SII-by-V20 interaction across grade ≥1, grade ≥2, and grade ≥3 endpoints. Grade ≥2 CIP was prespecified as the primary endpoint.These analyses were intended to improve risk stratification and generate hypotheses regarding host inflammatory status and radiation-dose susceptibility. They were not designed to establish a causal biological mechanism or a definitive individualized lung-dose constraint.Materials and methodsPatients and treatmentThis single-center retrospective study included 268 patients with stage IIB, III, or IVA esophageal squamous cell carcinoma who received PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors at the Affiliated Hospital of Hebei University between 2020 and 2023. Patients with stage IVA disease had no distant metastases. After exclusion of patients with interstitial lung disease, insufficient data, or follow-up <3 months (Supplementary Figure S2), 268 patients were included. Baseline SII was calculated as (neutrophils × platelets)/lymphocytes using the complete blood count obtained within 7 days before the first immunotherapy dose. The SII cutoff of 684.22 was derived from the Youden index for grade ≥2 CIP. Among the 268 patients, 154 (57.5%) subsequently received thoracic radiotherapy with an active local-control intent; no patient received palliative radiotherapy. Radiotherapy targeted the primary esophageal tumor and regional lymph nodes and was delivered using intensity-modulated radiotherapy with conventional fractionation. All 154 patients had received 2–4 cycles of induction immune-checkpoint-inhibitor–based treatment before radiotherapy. The median interval from the baseline blood sample to radiotherapy initiation was 84 days (IQR, 63–105 days). Immune checkpoint inhibitors were withheld during radiotherapy in all 154 patients and were not resumed after completion of radiotherapy. Concurrent chemotherapy was administered during radiotherapy in 108/154 patients (70.1%): 72 received a taxane or nab-paclitaxel plus a platinum agent and 36 received a fluoropyrimidine plus a platinum agent; 46 patients (29.9%) received radiotherapy without concurrent chemotherapy. All 154 patients completed the planned radiotherapy course. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Affiliated Hospital of Hebei University (approval No. HDFYLL-KY-2026-117), and the requirement for written informed consent was waived because of the retrospective design.EndpointsThe primary endpoint was grade ≥2 checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis (CIP). Any-grade (grade ≥1) CIP and severe (grade ≥3) CIP were secondary endpoints. Pneumonitis severity was graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE), version 5.0, and each patient was classified according to the highest grade reached during follow-up.Toxicity assessmentsPatients were monitored by outpatient symptom assessment and chest CT approximately every 2–3 months, with earlier imaging or additional evaluation when new respiratory symptoms occurred. CIP was diagnosed by multidisciplinary review involving pulmonologists, radiologists, and oncologists after consideration of symptoms, treatment timing, and serial imaging. In patients who received thoracic radiotherapy, an immune-related diagnosis required pulmonary abnormalities that extended beyond the radiation field or could not be fully explained by the dose distribution. candidates.title: Tocilizumab for acute exacerbation of rheumatic disease-associated interstitial lung disease: a real-world comparative cohort study.
candidates.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute exacerbation of rheumatic disease-associated interstitial lung disease (AE-RD-ILD) is life-threatening and is commonly managed with high-dose corticosteroids; however, no standardised evidence-based regimen has been established, particularly regarding adjunctive immunosuppressive therapy. We evaluated the effectiveness and safety of tocilizumab, an interleukin-6 receptor inhibitor, in hospitalised patients with AE-RD-ILD.
METHODS: In this single-centre ambispective observational cohort study conducted between January 2023 and December 2024, patients treated with tocilizumab (n=26) were compared with controls receiving corticosteroid-based conventional immunosuppression without tocilizumab (n=36). The primary outcome was investigator-defined objective composite clinical response (CR) at 24 weeks. Secondary outcomes included glucocorticoid exposure, oxygen discontinuation, radiological change, new acute exacerbation (AE) events, death or lung transplantation, and safety.
RESULTS: The 24-week CR rate was higher with tocilizumab than in controls (80.8% [21/26] vs. 13.9% [5/36], p<0.001), with a risk ratio of 5.82 (95% CI 2.52-13.40) and an adjusted hazard ratio of 10.43 (95% CI 3.71-29.28); estimates were consistent in sensitivity analyses addressing competing risks, guarantee-time bias and additional confounders. Tocilizumab was associated with lower cumulative prednisone dose (3955 vs. 5005 mg, p=0.016), lower minimum maintenance dose (10.0 vs. 15.0 mg/day, p<0.001), more frequent oxygen discontinuation (76.9% vs. 30.6%, p<0.001), and greater CT-assessed reduction in ILD extent (20% vs. 15%, p=0.045). New AE events and death or lung transplantation were numerically less frequent but not statistically significant. At least one infection occurred in 23.1% of tocilizumab-treated patients and 38.9% of controls (p=0.272). During longer follow-up, seven controls subsequently switched to tocilizumab because of recurrent or progressive respiratory disease.
